accuracy.evidence: Magma figures checked against USGS and BGS descriptions of magma types: basalt about 50% silica near 1150 °C (runny), andesite about 60% near 1000 °C, rhyolite 70% or more near 750 °C (very viscous); viscosity rises with silica and falls with temperature. Eruption facts checked against USGS event pages: Mauna Loa 27 Nov to 10 Dec 2022 (about 2 weeks, effusive), Kīlauea lower East Rift Zone May to early August 2018 (about 3 months of lava from fissures), Mount St Helens 18 May 1980 (ash column about 24 km), Pinatubo 15 June 1991 (ash column about 35 km), Vesuvius AD 79 burying Pompeii in ash and pumice, Fagradalsfjall March to September 2021 (effusive, visited by crowds). USGS states Mauna Loa is the largest active volcano on Earth. Mount Fuji and Vesuvius are stratovolcanoes. Statements about Hawaiʻi and Iceland use 'mostly' because basalt can explode when it meets water. Parameterised items (a*b, a-b, a+b) are whole positive numbers at every corner.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the slips reported in teacher guidance and USGS education notes: every volcano explodes (guide saying 1, m3, challenge tag all), runny lava builds steep cones (build-scene feedback, guide saying 3, challenge tag steep), a low, wide volcano must be small (guide saying 6, m5, challenge tag size), sticky magma is hotter (p5, challenge tag hot), sticky magma has no gas (p3, challenge tag nogas), and lava rivers being the main danger of an explosive eruption (guide saying 5, m6). The first predict ('Which lava flows farthest?') and the gas predict ('escape easily' vs 'get trapped') each offer the tempting wrong idea first.

lab_distinct.evidence: The lab is about this topic's mechanism: three lavas with their silica and temperature are poured on one vent and the mounds overlap so their spread can be compared; a draggable knob picks a magma and 'Let the gas out' shows bubbles escaping, half-stuck or trapped with a pressure gauge and ash; layers are stacked to match a dashed Mauna Loa shield and a Mount Fuji cone; six real eruptions are sorted from their clues. flagvolc (560) labels vent, crater and magma; flagvolcst (1012) sorts active, dormant and extinct and slides a plate over a hot spot. Neither has viscosity, gas pressure or shape-building. The lab_distinct gate keeps flag_erupt.js under 30% similar to every other lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner discovers each idea before the text confirms it: after pouring, the runny mound is visibly wide and low and the sticky one tall and narrow, with a tag saying 'spread far, stayed low'; in the gas scene the gauge stays green for runny magma and goes full red with an ash cloud for sticky; in the build scene choosing a runny flow for Mount Fuji is refused with 'A runny lava flow spreads wide and thin… that needs ash and sticky lava that pile up near the vent', and the layer readout reports 'wide, gentle slopes' or 'narrow, steep slopes'. Step-done lines then state the rule.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions, each with a tempting wrong option the lab then disproves: 'Which lava flows farthest?' (Sticky lava is tempting because it looks heavier; the pour shows runny reaching furthest), 'In thick, sticky magma, the gas bubbles…' ('escape easily' is disproved by the trapped bubbles and full gauge), and 'Which layers build a tall, steep cone?' ('Runny lava flows' is disproved when runny layers are refused for Mount Fuji). The reveal line names the right answer after the task.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge questions, each wrong option tagged with its own slip and a specific message: runny ('Runny magma lets gas bubble out, so it erupts gently'), nogas ('All magma holds some gas. Explosions need gas that is trapped'), steep, ashonly ('Mauna Loa erupts lava flows, not ash'), hot ('Sticky magma is cooler, not hotter'), flat, all ('Not all volcanoes explode… Hawaiʻi and Iceland') and size ('Shape shows lava type, not size'). The sort scene quotes the card's clue back, and the guide scene explains each fix.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short sentences and concrete comparisons (warm syrup, toothpaste, a fizzy drink) and score about 3.8 on the Flesch-Kincaid check (limit 6.5); adult text scores about 8 (limit 9.5). Technical words effusive, shield and composite are introduced once each with a plain meaning. Canvas text is dark on white or pale blue; long clues and guide sayings wrap onto two lines at phone width.

no_filler.evidence: Each kid paragraph adds one idea: what makes magma thick, gentle eruptions from escaping gas, explosive eruptions from trapped gas, and how eruptions build shield and cone shapes. The adult text gives the England and NGSS links with key terms, the silica and temperature figures with real examples, five named mistakes, and what the lab does. The content gate found no filler and under 12% overlap with every other lesson, including What Is a Volcano and Active, Dormant and Extinct.

mobile.evidence: Checked iPhone 13 screenshots in light and dark themes for every step part-way through and after Show me: the three magma cups fit across at about 110 px each with their silica and temperature lines, the gas knob is a 13 px-radius handle on a full-width track with a 28 px hit band, the layer buttons and eruption boxes are full half-width cards, eruption clues and guide sayings wrap inside their cards, and nothing is clipped. Every canvas action also has a button under the canvas.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a labelled button twin: 'Pour the runny basalt lava', 'Put sticky magma in the vent', 'Let the gas out', 'Add a layer of ash and sticky lava', 'This eruption was explosive', 'The guide made a slip'. Each change is announced through c.say and the canvas aria-label, and the challenge feedback is a polite live region. Right and wrong use ticks, crosses and words as well as colour. The walk gate's axe run is clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13.
